zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. [Dataset](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); [license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan remains authoritative for letters, typeface, marks, spacing and line division.

runs.text: xes meos mortos na lama, ou vaza.

lines.note: Xes completes pei at the end of f357, producing the fish comparison: half-dead in mud or mire. The opening is running text, not a second catchword.
This noun Naye denotes paralysis or disability of a limb. It is separate from the preceding page's verbal entry while sharing its bodily sense.
Nayoxi is identified only as a certain fish. The scan and gloss do not establish a precise modern species, so none is supplied.

runs.text: Duuida, ou enigma por palaura, ou eſ-

lines.note: Nazo is a riddle or enigma expressed orally, in writing, or by signs. The initial Portuguese word reads Duuida rather than OCR Dauida; eſ- begins eſcrito below.
Crito completes eſcrito, and ſinais adds nonverbal signs. Nazouo caquru begins the example of posing a riddle.
Eſte enigma completes the posing-riddle gloss. Nazouo toqu then supplies the complementary act of solving or explaining the riddle.
The riddle or difficulty is resolved. The scan supports duuida with two u letters rather than the OCR's shortened duida.
Nazodate is the proposing of an enigma. Na- begins the repeated noun in the example, retaining the printed physical division.
Zodateuo ſuru completes Nazodateuo ſuru, meaning to pose a riddle. No separate translation is printed on this short continuation.
Nazoraye means comparing or setting things alongside one another. The printed principal forms uru and eta belong to the verb, not the Portuguese gloss.
The example proposes describing the condition of Rocudǒ by a rough comparison. The Japanese form ends in nazoraye- and continues with te below.
Te completes nazorayete; mǒsǒzu is a historical prospective form of saying. Feiq. Lib. 4 supplies the citation, and Direi begins the Portuguese future-tense translation, correcting OCR Dirci.

runs.text: algũa comparação a maneira de Rocuſara aßi

lines.note: The Portuguese promises an approximate comparison and prints Rocuſara within its explanation, while the Japanese above reads Rocudǒ. This apparent mismatch is retained, not silently harmonized; the embedded name and its ſ/f distinction remain a nonblocking reading caveat.
Em großo completes the phrase meaning roughly or in broad outline. The printed ligature-like ß is retained rather than expanded to a modern spelling.

runs.text: Nazzumi, u, unda. Yuqicanuru. l, cutabi-

lines.note: Nazzumi is explained by Yuqicanuru and cutabiruru, inability to proceed and weariness. The intervening alternative marker is lowercase l, not OCR capital I; cutabi- continues below.

runs.text: Ir com repugnancia, ou canſar. Vt,

lines.note: Ruru completes cutabiruru. The Portuguese gives proceeding unwillingly or becoming tired, and Vt introduces the horse example.
Coma nazzumu describes a horse unable to go on. The Portuguese inability is completed with fatigue on the following line; the compact poderandar is retained.
Lo completes caualo; de canſaço gives the reason. A figurative example then begins Ienni naz-, concerning difficulty progressing in virtue, not an unrelated personal name.
Zumu completes nazzumu. The Portuguese explicitly interprets the example as advancing with difficulty in virtue, divided after vir-.
Tude completes virtude. Cu ni nazzumu applies the same difficulty to a verse or phrase, with the locative ni visibly separated.

runs.text: gũa parte, ou ſentença do verſo ſem poder ir

lines.note: The reader or composer gets stuck at a part or meaning of the verse and cannot proceed. The worn ending of parte is retained in the context of the complete printed word.
Por diante completes the inability to go further. It closes the verse example and is not part of the plant entry below.
Nazzuna is an herb of that name. The capital has the diagonal and uprights of N, correcting OCR Xazzuna; no modern species name is added to the canonical text.
Nazzuqe means naming or giving a name. The principal forms uru and eta are followed by the concise Portuguese Por nome.
Nazzuqi is the head, directly glossed Cabeça. It closes the A-section before the separate internal N ANTES DO E heading.

NE begins the new section and the example Neno toqi, the hour around midnight. The enlarged N spans this and the next physical row; the OCR dropped it and misclassified E as italic. The restored initial remains owned by this stable line ID.

runs.text: te pouco mais, ou menos ſegundo o modo de

lines.note: The midnight interval is approximate according to the Japanese way of counting hours. This row begins beside the enlarged N and remains indented; no extra text is inferred from the initial's overlap.
Completes the reference to the Japanese counting of hours. The wording contar das horas is retained as printed, without modernizing the construction.
Ne now means root. Nega ſaſu and Neuo ſaſu are the paired examples for putting out roots; the OCR's broken italic boundary inside Raiz is repaired to match the printed whole word.
The gloss reads Lãçar raizes, putting out roots, not OCR Lãear. Neuo fucǒ ſuru introduces the further example of putting down deep roots.
Tar completes Deitar, followed by fundas raizes. The visible u corrects OCR fandas and agrees with the Japanese fucǒ, deeply.
This Ne is price. Nega tatçu means that the price is established; the scan does not require adding punctuation after the final preço.
Itono nega tatta applies the established-price expression to silk. The Portuguese Abri ſe is retained with its printed spacing.
The reference is to the silk price being opened or fixed, also expressed as giving the pancada. Negatacai starts the contrast between a high and a low price.

runs.text: Ser o preço alto, ou baixo.

lines.note: Yaſui is the low-price alternative to tacai. The Portuguese explicitly contrasts high and low prices, completing the preceding example.

runs.text: Tom, ou ſoido, ou voz de paſſaros.

lines.note: Ne also means a tone, sound, or a bird's voice. This independent entry is distinct from the preceding root and price senses.
Neuo daſu describes a bird giving voice. The next example begins Ne-, repeated across the physical line break rather than treated as a separate headword.

runs.text: Cantar o paſſaro, veados, ou bi-

lines.note: Neuo naqu is applied to birds, deer, and small creatures. Bi- starts bichinhos, completed below; the literal Portuguese cantar is retained for this wider animal-voice usage.

Chinhos completes bichinhos. The quotation begins with water's bottom and years passing. Mizzuno is the chosen reading of the damaged Mizzui o: the surviving stem and available space support a worn n, while the Portuguese below supplies the water context. This restoration remains nonblocking and should receive human attention.

runs.text: uo furu cauazzu bacarizo neuoba naqu.

lines.note: The old frogs are the ones crying out: toxi-uo furu continues from the previous row, and neuoba naqu concerns their sound. The worn o and b in neuoba are retained from the surviving contours.

runs.text: As raãs velhas gritão no fũdo dagoa.

lines.note: Yax. is the printed citation label, and the Portuguese describes old frogs crying at the bottom of the water. A comparative public-domain Yashima text has the same frog-and-years passage, supporting the interpretation without establishing this copy's letters: [Kōwakamai, Yashima](https://ohta-masakazu.blog.jp/archives/29709494.html).
The verb Ne means sleeping, with nuru and eta as principal forms. Vtçumuqini begins the example for sleeping face downward.
Nuru completes the face-down example, glossed Dormir de bruços. Yoconeuo starts sleeping on one's side.
ſuru completes Yoconeuo ſuru, sleeping on the side. Auonoqini then introduces the opposite posture, lying face upward.
Nuru completes the face-up example, glossed as sleeping on the back. Marone and its alternative on the next row introduce sleeping without undressing.
Maruneuo ſuru completes the alternative expression for sleeping clothed and still girded. The last physical row and lower rule are both included in the crop.

runs.text: Raizes que eſtão fora da terra.

lines.note: Neagari refers to roots exposed above the ground. The line ends with a full stop after terra, not the OCR's hyphen; the next row starts an example rather than completing a divided word.
Neagarino daicon is a radish with its root exposed. The Portuguese word reads Rabãos, correcting OCR Ralãos; its b is supported by the ascender.
Completes the exposed-radish-root description. Neagarino ma- begins the second example, whose pine-tree word is divided after ma-.

runs.text: Pinheiro que tem as raizes fora, ou

lines.note: Tçu completes matçu, pine. The Portuguese explains that the pine's roots are outside the soil or exposed, with the final adjective below.
Deſcubertas completes the exposed-root gloss. The short line belongs to the pine example, not the sticky-substance entry that follows.
Nebai describes something viscous or sticky. Both Portuguese adjectives support the physical sense that is then extended to human behaviour.
Nebai tçuchi is sticky earth. A second Nebai begins the description of a person, continued on the next row.
Fito completes Nebai fito, a soft or slow-moving person. The human application is figurative rather than a claim that the person is literally adhesive.

Nebacuchi is a person who speaks very slowly. The capital N corrects OCR X; Peſſoa is chosen for the damaged Portuguese noun, whose e is weak between P and the long-s pair, rather than retaining the meaningless Piſſoa.
Nebacuchina and nebacuchina mono have the same slow-speaking meaning. The repeated Idem refers directly to the preceding person-description.
Nebacuji is a very protracted lawsuit or dispute. The Portuguese demanda gives the legal-dispute sense, not a generic request.
Nebagatai describes something hard yet pliable. The following contrast with brittleness controls the sense of meneauel and prevents interpreting hardness alone.
The material is not brittle. Nebagatai- begins an example modifying qi, wood, on the next physical row; its terminal hyphen is retained.
Qi completes the hard-wood example. Permet. introduces the figurative application to a person, beginning Ne- at the right edge.
Nebagatai fito describes a person severe by nature. The printed word is natureza, correcting OCR natareza; this severity is balanced by the qualification below.

runs.text: & brando, ou vagaroſo por outra via.

lines.note: The person is also gentle or slow in another respect. This apparent combination is explicitly printed and should not be simplified to a single modern personality adjective.
Nebaracaxi is referred to the preferred form Nebaxi through Meliùs. The first form's aita is abraded but supported by the remaining letters; both verb forms stay in roman type.

runs.text: Fazer basto, & viſcoſo, ou engroſar como

lines.note: The definition is making something thick or viscous, like the mixture below. Viſcoſo and engroſar repair the garbled OCR; the apparent comma after en was the surviving descender of g, not sentence punctuation.
Polme supplies the example of a thick paste or batter. This short row completes the thickening verb rather than defining a separate Japanese noun.

runs.text: O engroſſarſe couſa liquida, ou rala.

lines.note: Nebari is the thickening of a liquid or thin substance. The scan reads liquida, correcting the corrupted iquãda; no tilde is supplied to that word.
Nebariga deqita means that thickness or stickiness has developed. The Portuguese ends ou, without the OCR's spurious final s, and continues with baſto.
Baſto completes the thickening gloss. Cotobani nebariga deqita introduces a figurative application to someone's words, translated from Ia onward.

runs.text: ha por onde pegar ao que condeſcende hũ

lines.note: There is now something to get hold of in the words of someone beginning to yield. The initial is ha, not OCR ba; hũ retains its abbreviation tilde.
The person yields a little after much resistance. This explains the figurative example rather than the literal texture of a liquid.
The verb Nebari means becoming thick, applied to a liquid or thin substance. The principal part atta is retained; this is the intransitive counterpart of the thickening verbs above.
Nebatçuchi is sticky earth. Its compound form contrasts with the separately written Nebai tçuchi example earlier in the column.
Nebatçuqi describes something adhering to the hands. The material causing the adhesion is specified on the following line.

runs.text: couſa viſcoſa que ſe trata com ellas.

lines.note: The material is a viscous substance being handled. Ellas refers back to the hands, not to a second group of objects.
Nebaxi refers the reader back to Nebaracaxi. Vide is italic apparatus; the repeated Japanese verb remains roman rather than being absorbed into the gloss.
Nebiye is becoming chilled while sleeping at night. Ne begins the example, divided from biye on the following row without an added hyphen.
Nebiye xita is rendered in the first person as becoming cold during sleep at night. The historical form Es frieime and its spacing are preserved rather than replaced by modern spelling.

runs.text: Não eſtar em ſeu a cordo

lines.note: Nebôqe means not being fully aware while drowsy. The gloss reads eſtar, with a, correcting OCR ester; the circumflex on the headword is retained.
Toſquenejando completes the drowsiness description. This historical Portuguese form is not modernized to a more familiar synonym for dozing.

Neburi is glossed Lãber, 'lick,' and the preferred cross-reference is Nemuri, not the nearby sleeping headwords. The second pass reveals the thin surviving stem and foot of an abraded first t before the clear second t: the chosen reading is utta rather than OCR uta. The restoration is retained with a damaged-glyph caveat; the scan, not expected morphology alone, supports it.
Neburitçuqi describes adhering or attaching oneself by licking. The following dog example shows the action in a behavioural context.

The dog licks and catches hold with its mouth, seeking the master's favour. The damaged sequence reads xujinno, with the possessive no following xujin, rather than OCR xujiono; qi continues into the next row's uo.
Uo completes qiuo, and toru monogia states the dog's tendency to seek favour. Fab. is an upright citation label; its full stop is not part of the following italic translation.

runs.text: do, & pegando com a boca contenta ao ſenhor.

lines.note: The dog pleases its master by licking and taking hold with its mouth. This completes the example rather than defining literal adhesive strength.
Nebuto is an abscess or swelling, as clarified by the paired Portuguese postema. The historical Leicenſo is retained; Nebu- begins the example of developing one.

The opening toga deqita completes Nebutoga deqita, 'a boil appeared.' The Portuguese says that a leicenſo arose on the speaker. The very tight humleicenſo is retained from the aligned text after enlargement rather than imposing a modern word space; the e of me is abraded but readable from its remaining strokes.

runs.text: Couſa de voz großa como frauta, ou

lines.note: Nebutoi describes a deep or full voice or instrumental tone. A flute and organ are the examples, not a physical width measurement of the object.
The instrumental example pairs fuye with xacufachi. Both Japanese instrument words belong to the standalone example rather than embedded Portuguese terminology.

runs.text: Frauta que tem o ſom großo, ou cheo.

lines.note: The flute has a thick or full sound. Großo and cheo complete the acoustic, not physical, interpretation of Nebutoi.
Neccu is explained by Atçuqi curuximi, suffering from heat. The Portuguese Tormẽto de quẽtura confirms that explanation while preserving its abbreviation tildes.
The first Neco is simply a cat. Its separate line and full stop distinguish it from the identically spelled bellows component below.

runs.text: Pelle, ou couro que està dentro nos fo

lines.note: The second Neco is a leather piece inside a bellows. Fo is the beginning of foles, completed by the restored physical row below; no hyphen is supplied where the scan has none.

runs.text: les do ferreiro que ſerue de tapar o buraco pera

lines.note: This omitted body row completes foles do ferreiro and explains the leather's function: closing the hole so air will not escape when the bellows are compressed. The sentence continues on f359; the separate lower que is a catchword, not a substitute for this row.
